spots.justification: Heads-up the button acts first before the flop, and AA is the best starting hand in the game. Raising builds a bigger pot while your hand strength is at its peak, and you keep position after the flop.
Against a single opponent, KJo is well above the average hand the big blind can hold. Raise to take the initiative and use your position on every later street.

72o is one of the weakest starting hands, with no pair, no flush help and almost no straight help. Even heads-up its equity against a big blind that defends is too low to add more chips, so fold the small blind.
83o makes few strong hands and is often dominated by the hands the big blind keeps. Its poor hand strength means completing or raising loses more than the half bet you give up by folding.
The button only completed, so its hand is usually capped below a premium pair, and KK is far ahead. Raising for value builds the pot while your hand strength is strongest.
AKo dominates most of the aces and kings a limping button holds. Raise to take the initiative and charge those weaker hands while your equity edge is large.
Checking is free and closes the betting, so there is no reason to fold 72o here. Its hand strength is too poor to raise, but a free flop costs nothing and keeps your equity in the pot.
Q4o is too weak to build a pot while acting first after the flop, yet seeing that flop costs nothing. Check and let the board decide, since folding a free option gives away equity for no reason.
You completed and the big blind raised, but AA is ahead of every hand it can hold. Re-raise to build the pot while your hand strength is at its highest, and you keep position after the flop.
A5o holds an ace, which is often the best high card heads-up, and the raise still leaves good pot odds on one more bet. It is not strong enough to re-raise, so call and play the flop in position.
The big blind raises a wide range heads-up, and K7o has more than enough equity against it at 3 to 1. Call and play the hand with position on every later street.
J9s makes pairs, straights and flushes, and you act last after the flop. One small bet for a pot of 12 chips gives good pot odds, so call rather than fold.
The big blind re-raised your button open, but its range is wide and KK beats almost all of it. Cap the betting with a raise for value while your hand strength is far ahead.
K8o holds a king that is often best against a wide heads-up re-raiser, and the pot is already large. The pot odds make one more call clearly right, but it is not strong enough to raise again.
Even A2o holds an ace, which beats many of the hands a heads-up button re-raises with. The pot is large and you need only one more bet, so those pot odds justify a call but not a raise.
The button's re-raise shows a strong hand, but AA is never behind before the flop. Raise again for value to put the most chips in while your hand strength is at its peak.
The button raises a wide range heads-up, and AQo is well ahead of most of it. Re-raise for value to take the initiative, even though you will be out of position after the flop.

With a full bet already in, you need only one more bet and the pot odds are excellent. K5o holds a king, which is often best against a wide button range, so call rather than fold, but do not re-raise.
A heads-up button raises most of its hands, and J6o has enough equity against that range at 3 to 1. Call to close the action instead of giving up the big blind you already posted.
AKs is ahead of almost every hand a heads-up button raises with. Re-raise for value and take the initiative, which makes up for playing out of position after the flop.
AA is the strongest starting hand, so open-raise even with five players left to act. The raise builds the pot and takes the initiative while your hand strength is far ahead.
From the first seat five players act behind you, and K7o is easily dominated by better kings. Its hand strength is too weak to open from this position, so fold.
Folded to you in the hijack, AJo is ahead of most hands the four players behind will hold. Open-raise to take the initiative and often win the blinds.
KQo is a strong broadway hand, and only the button and blinds remain behind you in the cutoff. Raise first in, since good position and two high cards make it profitable.
Even in the cutoff, 93o has too little hand strength to open, because the button can call or raise behind you and keep position. Fold and wait for a better hand.
On the button only the blinds remain, and K5s holds a king plus flush chances. Raise to steal the blinds, and you keep position on every later street if one of them calls.

In the small blind 76s is too weak to raise against the big blind, but the half bet already posted makes completing cheap. Its suited, connected cards give good implied odds when they make a straight or flush.
A limper usually holds a medium hand, and AKo dominates many of them. Raise to isolate the limper and take the initiative into a heads-up pot where your hand strength is well ahead.
66 rarely wins a big pot unless it flops a set, so it wants a cheap multiway flop. Limping behind keeps the price low and the implied odds high when the set arrives.
QQ is far ahead of two limpers, who usually hold medium hands. Raise for value and to thin the field, and you will have position on everyone after the flop.
85o has low cards and no flush chance, so even with the button's position it plays poorly in a limped pot. Fold rather than pay a full bet with such low hand strength.
A5s can make the nut flush or a wheel straight, and completing costs only half a bet with a limper in. Those implied odds make a call right, while a raise would bloat a pot you play out of position.
The small blind completed and nobody raised, so you can check for free with 72o. Its hand strength is far too low to raise, but folding a free flop would only throw away equity.
AKs is ahead of almost every hand that limps, so raise from the big blind rather than check. The raise builds a pot you are favoured to win, which outweighs acting early with worse position.
Only aces beat KK, so a single early raise is no reason to slow down. Re-raise to play heads-up with the initiative, building a pot where your hand strength is far ahead.
An early raiser holds strong hands, and KJo is often dominated by the aces and better kings in that range. Its equity is too low to call or re-raise, so fold.
AKo is ahead of most of an opening range and blocks the aces and kings that beat it. Re-raise for value to play heads-up with the initiative.
A9o is a weak ace that loses badly to the better aces an opener holds, and it will rarely win a big pot. Its equity against a raise is poor, so fold.
QQ is a premium pair that beats most of a single opener's range. Re-raise to isolate the raiser, and you will keep position on every street after the flop.
K9o is dominated by the better kings and aces a raiser holds, and it has no flush chance to make up for it. Even with position, its equity is too low to continue, so fold.
You limped, then a raise and a call followed, and AA is ahead of every hand in the pot. Re-raise for value to build a large pot while your hand strength is at its best.
Several bets are already in the pot, so 55 needs only one more to try to flop a set. The pot odds and implied odds make calling right, while a re-raise would run into better pairs.
An open and a call have built the pot, and KK is ahead of both players' likely hands. Re-raise for value and to take the initiative into the flop.
44 usually needs a set to win, and with two players already in, the implied odds are good. Calling one more bet is right, but its hand strength is too low to re-raise.
K9o is dominated by the strong kings and aces that raise and call, and an offsuit hand rarely makes a flush to escape. Fold, because its equity in a multiway pot is poor.
AKs is ahead of most of the raiser's and caller's hands and makes strong pairs and flushes. Re-raise for value from the button, where you keep position for the whole hand.
JTs makes straights and flushes that win big multiway pots, and the button keeps position after the flop. With a raise and a call in, the pot odds make calling clearly better than folding.
Your open was re-raised, but AA beats every hand the re-raiser holds. Raise again for value, since your hand strength cannot be dominated before the flop.
99 is a solid pair you opened, and the re-raise means the pot is already large. The pot odds make calling one more bet right, but its hand strength is not high enough to raise again.
77 opened from the hijack and now faces a re-raise, but you need only one more bet. The pot odds and the chance of a set make calling right, while raising would overrate its hand strength.
QTs was a fine cutoff open and keeps its flush and straight chances, and a re-raise against a cutoff open is often light. The pot odds on one more bet make calling right, but it is too weak to raise.
A blind re-raising a button open has a wide range, and AKo is ahead of nearly all of it. Raise again for value, and you keep position after the flop.
JTs makes many straights and flushes, and with the pot already large you need only one more bet. The pot odds justify a call even out of position, but its hand strength is not enough to raise again.

A limper who re-raises usually holds a big pair or ace-king, and AA is ahead of all of them. Raise again for value, since your equity edge is largest now and you will be out of position on every later street.
AKs is well ahead of a button opening range. Re-raise for value and to push the big blind out, so you play heads-up and offset being out of position.
QQ is ahead of even a tight early opening range. Re-raise from the small blind to get heads-up with the initiative, since calling would let the big blind join a pot you play out of position.
K9o is dominated by many opening hands, and calling from the small blind leaves you out of position with the big blind still to act. Its equity does not cover those problems, so fold.
AQs is ahead of most cutoff opens and makes strong pairs and nut flushes. Re-raise for value rather than just calling, even though you will be out of position after the flop.
With a full bet in, you need one more bet into a pot that lays three and a half to one. K5s has a king and flush chances, so those pot odds make defending by calling clearly right.

T8s connects with many flops through straights and flushes, and the button opens a wide range. Closing the action with good pot odds, calling is right, though the hand is not strong enough to re-raise.

Against a button steal KTs is ahead of much of the raiser's range, and you close the action getting three and a half to one. Those pot odds and its flush and straight chances make calling clear, even out of position.
72o wins too rarely to call, even with the good pot odds the big blind gets. Its equity against a button raise is too low, so fold and save the bet.
KK is the second-best starting hand, so open-raise even with eight players behind you. The raise starts building a pot your hand strength is likely to win.
Under the gun at a full table, KJo is often dominated by the aces and kings that wake up behind you. Its hand strength is too low to open from such an early position, so fold.
AKo is one of the strongest starting hands and plays well against the players left behind the middle position. Raise first in to take the initiative and build a pot you are likely to win.
T8o has modest high cards and no flush chance, and five players still act after the lojack. Its hand strength is too weak to open from this position, so fold.
From the hijack every suited ace opens, and A2s can make the nut flush or a wheel straight. With few players behind, its equity and the chance to win the blinds make a raise right.
55 is a pair, which is ahead of most unpaired hands the button and blinds hold. Raise first in from the cutoff to take the blinds often and keep position when called.
On the button only the blinds remain, and K4s holds a king plus flush potential. Raise to attack the blinds, since position on every later street helps a hand like this.

KJs is well ahead of a random big blind hand, so raising from the small blind takes the initiative and often wins the blinds at once. When called, its suited broadway cards make strong pairs and draws.
An under-the-gun limper rarely holds a premium hand, and AKs is ahead of most limping hands. Raise to isolate the limper and play with the initiative.
55 wins big when it flops a set and loses little when it misses, so a cheap multiway pot suits it. Overlimp behind the limper for the implied odds instead of raising.
K9o is dominated by the better kings a limper can hold, and many players still act behind you. Its hand strength is too low to call or raise, so fold.
QQ is far ahead of two limpers, whose ranges rarely include stronger pairs. Raise for value and to thin the field before the flop, taking the initiative.

44 rarely wins unimproved, but behind a limper the price to see a flop is low and a set can win a big pot. Overlimp for the implied odds rather than raise a small pair that plays poorly against callers.
AQo dominates many of the hands that limp, and the button keeps position for the whole hand. Raise to isolate the limpers and take the initiative.
44 needs to flop a set, and completing costs only half a bet with two limpers already in. Those implied odds make completing right, even though you act first after the flop.
J4o has poor hand strength, so there is no reason to raise from the big blind. Checking is free, so take the flop and keep whatever equity the hand has.
Even an under-the-gun raise, the tightest range at the table, is behind AA. Re-raise for value to build the pot and play heads-up with the initiative.
KQo looks strong, but against an under-the-gun raise it is dominated by ace-king, ace-queen and big pairs. Its equity is too low to continue, so fold.
TT is often ahead of the overcards in an early raiser's range but behind its big pairs. Call to see a flop with good pot odds and implied odds, rather than re-raise into a strong range.

Against an early opener AKo dominates the ace-queen, ace-jack and king-queen hands in that range and is close to even against the middle pairs. Re-raise to get heads-up with the initiative and charge the hands it dominates.
K9s is dominated by the better kings and aces in an early raiser's range. Its equity is too low against that strong range, even suited, so fold.
AKs is ahead of nearly all of a middle-position opening range and plays well heads-up. Re-raise to isolate the raiser and keep position after the flop.
22 is the smallest pair and rarely wins unless it flops a set, while the button and blinds can still raise behind you. Without enough implied odds against a single raiser, fold.

88 is ahead of much of a hijack's opening range once the cutoff folds, and the button keeps position for the whole hand. Re-raise to isolate the opener and charge the blinds, taking the initiative instead of just calling.
KK is ahead of both the raiser and the caller in almost every case. Re-raise for value to build a large pot while your hand strength is far ahead.
77 rarely wins a big pot unless it flops a set, and a raise and a call give good implied odds. Calling is right, but its hand strength is too low to re-raise into two players.
KQo is often dominated by the hands that raise and call, and an offsuit hand rarely improves to something strong. Its equity in a multiway pot is too low, so fold.
AKs is ahead of most hands that open and call, and it makes the nut flush when its suit comes. Re-raise for value to build the pot while your hand strength leads.

AJs dominates many of the weaker aces and broadway hands a flat caller holds, and its suit adds flush outs in a multiway pot. Call rather than re-raise, since the opener's middle-position range holds enough bigger aces and pairs to make a raise risky with players still to act.

ATs plays well in a multiway pot, where its flush and broadway straight outs pay off more often than its high card. Call with position on both players rather than re-raise, because a lojack opener still holds many aces that beat yours.
KJo is dominated by many raising and calling hands and seldom makes a strong hand in a multiway pot. Its equity does not justify another bet, so fold.
AKo is ahead of the raiser and the caller most of the time, and the button keeps position on both. Re-raise for value to build the pot with your hand strength advantage.
AKs is among the best hands against a re-raise, and it blocks the aces and kings that beat it. Raise again for value with this hand strength rather than just calling.
99 was a sound under-the-gun open, and the pot is now large enough that one more bet is cheap. Those pot odds make calling right, but the pair is not strong enough to raise again.
KQs plays well after the flop with its high cards and flush chances, and you need only one more bet. The pot odds make calling right, but it is too weak to raise again against a re-raise.
A re-raise from the button is often wide, and KK is ahead of almost all of it. Raise again for value while your hand strength is far ahead.
JTs makes straights and flushes, and a re-raise against a cutoff open often comes from a wide range. With the pot this large, the pot odds make calling right.
QTo has two broadway cards, and a blind re-raising your button steal often holds a wide range. The pot odds on one more bet and your position make calling right.
QQ is ahead of most of the big blind's re-raising range. Raise again for value even out of position, since your hand strength is well ahead.

The limper's re-raise points to big pairs and strong aces, so AJs is too often behind to raise again. One more small bet into a pot of 22 chips is a cheap price, and the pot odds plus your flush and top-pair outs make calling clear.
KK is far ahead of a button opening range. Re-raise for value and to push out the big blind, which helps when you must play out of position.
AKo is well ahead of a lojack opening range. Re-raise to play heads-up with the initiative, since calling from the small blind invites the big blind in.

An under-the-gun raiser holds a strong range, and K9s is dominated by the bigger kings and aces in it. Calling leaves you out of position with the big blind still to act, and its equity is too low to re-raise, so fold.
T8o is an offsuit hand with weak cards, and from the small blind you would play it out of position. Its hand strength is too low to call or re-raise, so fold.
AKs is ahead of most hijack opening hands. Re-raise for value from the big blind to build a pot your hand strength is favoured to win.
With a full bet already in, you need one more bet into a pot that lays good pot odds. K6s has a king and flush chances, so call rather than fold, though it is too weak to re-raise.
T9s connects well with many flops for straights and flushes. Closing the action with good pot odds, call and see the flop rather than give up the blind.
94o is a weak offsuit hand that rarely makes anything strong. Even with a full bet already in, its equity against a hijack raise is too low, so fold.

We called an early open and the big blind re-raised, so two strong ranges are ahead of us and none of the raises is ours. A9o is often dominated by bigger aces, so its hand strength is too low to put in another bet; fold.

An open and a re-raise came before us, so the ranges are strong, but our blind is in and the pot odds on one more bet are good. A pair of eights can flop a set and win a big pot, so call rather than fold, though it is too weak to raise.

A pair of aces is the strongest starting hand and is ahead of every range that opens and re-raises. Raise again to build the pot while our hand strength is far ahead, and we keep position after the flop.
